issues.issue: Original first-edition Chapter XCII is stable editorial XCIII due an earlier duplicated printed numeral; retain both identifiers.
Chapter XCII begins below the Captive or Slave divider on PDF498/printed464 and continues through all of PDF499 and PDF500, ending before Chapter XCIII on PDF501.
Astrological associations with witchcraft, possession, 'fore-speaking' or spirits are authorial historical supernatural claims; the source provides no evidence those causes exist.
These passages explicitly presuppose prior suspicion and include flexible disjunctions; they cannot be scored as blinded case diagnoses.
The six opening reciprocal house-lord placements are distinct logical alternatives, not independent observed patients or events.
The first/twelfth common ruler allegedly creates non-natural sickness; no laboratory, clinical or recorded patient verification exists.
Saturn retrograde in twelfth, seventh or eighth plus Moon lord sixth applying to Saturn is a compounded historical claim requiring chart reconstruction.
The first-edition source associates thought disturbance with spirit oppression; this must not be presented as a clinical or psychiatric diagnosis.
An astrologically inferred direction of a suspected witch is not evidence for locating or accusing an actual individual.
The PDF498–499 physical text seam continues a combust-ascendant claim; it does not create an extra judgment.
Third house versus sixth house accusations implicate neighbors, relatives, hired workers, vendors or nurses without independent identification.
The historical descriptions of women, nurses and drinking associates are stigmatizing stereotype, not justified social risk guidance.
The tenth-house 'hand of God' passage is a separate religious attribution rather than a supernatural finding.
The twelfth-ruler in first, Mars/Saturn placement and Moon opposition conditions overlap others; preserve duplicate terminology without double-counting any real case.
Derived-house reassignments for cattle are mathematical convention in Lilly, not veterinary evidence of witchcraft.
The heading 'Naturall Remedies for Witchcraft' is an unnumbered historical subsection within XCII, not new numbered chapter.
The author first assumes his horary reading can identify a witch and times the ritual to a suspect's whereabouts; no valid perpetrator identification exists.
Household rituals involving hot tiles, fire or bodily fluids pose burn, contamination and fire risks; do not treat them as contemporary therapeutic instructions.
Cattle-hair, ashes, burial-direction and household thatch stories are symbolic rituals, not experimentally supported veterinary treatments.
Variations using heated metal objects and bodily fluids have no authenticated human outcomes and may present significant physical hazards.
The author links the supposed procedure's efficacy to a lunar phase without a calibrated prospective test.
His asserted sympathy mechanism is a historical idea, not established causal mechanism or licensed medical procedure.
Lilly's 'several experiments' is a retrospective author claim lacking first-person patient records, controls, denominators, dated successes, harms or blinded comparisons.
The final Latin maxim has uncertain transcription/philological meaning; do not infer his confidence or experiment standards beyond the explicit English.
The next chapter's horse-recovery square horoscope (original PDF501) is a separate dated case and cannot verify the witchcraft claims.

The subsequent horse passage itself reports actual return after three days versus a forecast of one or two; that negative timing discrepancy belongs to next chapter and should be independently audited.
The original page scans are source witnesses; this pass does not assert a complete second independent diplomatic transcription or recalculated horary parity.

No source-based accusation, clinical diagnosis, spiritual possession claim, symptom treatment recommendation, empirically validated prediction, or runtime rule promotion follows from the historical extraction.
